articles.title: Club Kid review – Jordan Firstman’s heartfelt comedy is irresistible
articles.summary: New York film festival: the actor impresses with a directorial debut about a club rat who discovers he is father to a 10-year-old boy. In a grungy backroom of a Brooklyn warehouse, a group of glamorously dishevelled clubbers raise their voices in a secular chat. “What do we want? Drugs!
body: Peter (Firstman) is the life of the party and has been running his raucous Club Labor for over a decade. He always gets the drugs in, rolls up with the best-dressed crew and knows everyone. But the comedowns – bed-rot days of anime porn, takeout and self-loathing – aren’t getting any easier, and he is screwing up opportunities for the party to get to the next level. “You’re a fucking child,” spits his business partner Sophie ( Cara Delevingne in her best performance yet) after he shows up to a lunch meeting with potential investors straight from the rave.

After initially setting strict boundaries to his nightlife friends’ interactions with Arlo (“No talk about dicks or drugs,” he hisses), Peter finds a way to share his life with his son. He brings Arlo record shopping in the East Village staple A1, and introduces him to a DJ friend named Saffron (the luminous Saturn Risin9) who teaches the kid to use mixing decks. It’s the kind of set-up that feels too good to be true, and it is not plain sailing for father and son, with greater challenges to come.

body: Luca Guadagnino ’s “ Artificial ” premiered at the New York Film Festival Monday night, and early reviews have members of the film press championing the Sam Altman-centered movie as a “provocative,” “visceral corporate drama” and the director’s “best film in a decade.”

Editor Eric Kohn called the film a “pitch-perfect dark comedy.” “Andrew Garfield walks a fine line between movie monster, buffoonish mogul, and evil genius. A fun/scary ride that embodies the paradox at its center,” he wrote on X.

“Guadagnino guts Silicon Valley with his obsessive pulse & a powerful farce in which Andrew Garfield completely shines,” wrote film critic Jairo Jiménez. “A feverish, visceral corporate drama that proves what is truly artificial was never in the machines, but in the boardroom. An essential film.”
Variety’s Clayton Davis wrote that “Artificial” is “Guadagnino’s best film in a decade” and “Andrew Garfield and Yura Borisov soar to new heights. Loved.”

articles.title: ‘Exceptionally crafted’: why Little Shop of Horrors is my feelgood movie
articles.summary: The latest in our series of writers’ favorite comfort films is a tribute to the lovably quirky 80s musical. The key to a feelgood movie, beyond the necessary rewatchability, is familiarity – the real kind that lets you look away or fall asleep without doubting your affection.
body: The first act of Funny Girl? A near-flawless parade of showstoppers, Barbra Streisand as Fanny Brice having the time of her life falling in love. I’ve probably seen it 200 times. The second act … well, who ever cared about her husband’s gambling addiction?

At just 94 minutes, Frank Oz’s film of Little Shop of Horrors doesn’t suffer from that sharp of a drop-off. The cult 1982 musical that translates to the screen is already a pretty perfect piece; a hilarious send-up of B-movies with glorious songs by Howard Ashman and Alan Menken, the duo whose music would soon ignite the Disney Renaissance. The whole thing is a miracle of dumpster diving: adapting an almost-forgotten 1960 movie by indie legend Roger Corman, who didn’t even bother to copyright his low-budget horror comedy.

But enough history. Little Shop, the movie, begins, and you’re there: Skid Row, the derelict, richly detailed cityscape with the lovingly obvious soundstage feel that most art departments left behind sometime in the 90s in favor of realism. The son of puppeteers and the first to perform both Yoda and Miss Piggy, Oz had individuality and scene-setting in his DNA.
points: The latest in our series of writers’ favorite comfort films is a tribute to the lovably quirky 80s musical.
The key to a feelgood movie, beyond the necessary rewatchability, is familiarity – the real kind that lets you look away or fall asleep without doubting your affection.

articles.title: Blue Planet and Gandhi composer George Fenton dies aged 76
articles.summary: The musician received five Oscar nominations, and soundtracked dozens of memorable nature films.
body: Composer George Fenton, whose work included music for films such as Gandhi, Groundhog Day and The Fisher King, as well as TV shows like Planet Earth and Bergerac, has died at the age of 76.
The prolific musician received five Oscar nominations for his film scores, including those for The Remains of the Day and Cry Freedom.

His work on the BBC TV show Blue Planet also earned awards from the Baftas, Emmy Awards and Ivor Novellos; and he also composed theme music for BBC News programmes such as Newsnight and Breakfast Time.
In a statement, Fenton's family said: "We are very sad to announce that George Fenton passed away unexpectedly today."

articles.title: Post your questions for Sofia Coppola
articles.summary: A new documentary by Eleanor Coppola goes behind the scenes on her daughter’s 2006 punk classic, Marie Antoinette. To mark its release, Sofia Coppola will be taking your questions. To say that Sofia Coppola grew up on screen would be an understatement.
body: In between came small roles in several of her dad’s films, including 1983’s The Outsiders and Rumble Fish, 1984’s The Cotton Club and 1986’s Peggy Sue Got Married, in which she played Kathleen Turner’s younger sister Nancy. She also popped up all over 1990s music videos, playing a wild-eyed Joan Crawford in Sonic Youth’s 1990 Mildred Pierce, a troubled drifter in the Black Crowes’ 1992 Sometimes Salvation, one of Madonna’s clubbing friends in 1992’s Deeper and Deeper, and an injured gymnast in the Chemical Brothers’ 1997 Elektrobank, directed by her then-boyfriend Spike Jonze.

Although this brings up loads of questions you may well like to ask her already – what was it like growing up in the Coppola household, with Nicolas Cage as her cousin? – it’s probably what happened when she switched to behind the camera that will intrigue you most.

articles.title: Jeffrey Archer: successful novelist, disgraced politician and convicted liar
articles.summary: Politician and best-selling author whose career was mired in scandal and disgrace.
body: As many have observed, Jeffrey Archer, who has died aged 86, led a life as colourful as the plot in one of his novels.
He was, at one time or other, a senior Conservative politician, a best-selling author, a peer of the realm, and a convicted perjurer.
Possessed of huge drive, vast wealth and immense personal charm, Archer bounced back from disaster and, more than once, rebuilt a shattered life.
But for all his talents, he will be remembered as a man affected by a defective moral compass, whose public humiliation was entirely self-inflicted.

articles.title: Five Takeaways from Metallica’s “No Repeat Weekend” Sphere Shows
articles.summary: Night two mirrored the geometry of opening night without repeating a song, reached deep into the band's catalog and saved one spectacular “Enter Sandman” for last
body: The second half of the band’s first “No Repeat Weekend” showed no signs of losing momentum, with 22 more shows still to come through March 2027.
James Hetfield appeared acutely aware of the investment fans were making. “We’re grateful you’ve taken the time, energy and the cash,” he told the crowd Saturday.

Metallica isn’t simply asking its audience to come back; it has to make a solid argument for the second ticket. After 15 completely different songs and another two hours of entirely different visuals, night two felt carefully composed from beginning to end, built to reward the faithful while delivering a spectacle enormous enough to entrance the merely curious.

Thursday featured “Sad but True,” “Nothing Else Matters,” “Seek & Destroy,” “Master of Puppets” and the nearly 10-minute “…And Justice for All.” Saturday ripped through “The Unforgiven,” “For Whom the Bell Tolls,” “One” — also from …And Justice for All — and “Enter Sandman,” arguably the band’s biggest hit. Saturday sweetened the heavy honey pot with deeper pulls as “Devil’s Dance,” from Reload, returned for the first time since 2008, while Load epic “The Outlaw Torn” was back after last appearing in 2019.
